raw.answer: The case asked whether a rule in the implementing regulations of the Estate and Gift Tax Act was unconstitutional. The rule starts the estate tax filing period for a person declared dead by a court from the date of the court's judgment. The court held that the rule does not conflict with Article 19 of the Constitution.
raw.held: The regulation that counts the estate tax filing period for a person declared dead from the date of the judgment declaring death fits the law's purpose and the nature of such cases, and does not conflict with Article 19 of the Constitution.

points.text: The Estate and Gift Tax Act requires filing within six months of the death of a person who left property. A declaration of death also ends a person's legal capacity, just as natural death does.
A declared death is presumed to have occurred at a time fixed in the judgment, which must be before the court announces it.
Before the judgment is announced, it is not settled whether the missing person's property is an estate. Taxpayers cannot file, and the tax authority cannot begin to assess the tax.

So counting the filing period from the judgment date lets both taxpayers and the tax authority follow the rule. It fits the law's purpose and the nature of the matter, and does not conflict with Article 19.
The court added that the start date of the filing period and the basis for valuing the estate affect the duty to pay tax. It said these should be set by law to avoid disputes.
On the question about the proviso to Article 10, paragraph 1 of the Act, the court said Interpretation No. 311 had already addressed it.

raw.answer: The case asked whether teachers at public schools, including those who also hold administrative posts, are covered by the Civil Servants Service Act. The court decided that teachers hired under a teaching contract are not covered as civil servants under Article 24 of that Act. A teacher who also takes on a school administrative post is covered for that administrative work.
raw.held: Public school teachers hired by contract are not 'civil servants' under Article 24 of the Civil Servants Service Act, but a teacher who also holds an administrative post is covered for that post. Full-time teachers still may not take outside jobs unless other rules allow it, under Article 34 of the Educational Personnel Employment Act.

points.text: Contract-hired teachers do teaching and research work based on a contract, which differs from civil servants who carry out duties set by law under a superior's supervision.
So contract-hired teachers are not civil servants under Article 24 of the Civil Servants Service Act.
If such a teacher also takes a school administrative post, the Act still applies to that administrative work.
The court's earlier Interpretation Yuan-Jie No. 2986 said contract-hired staff were not covered. The court supplements it as to contract-hired teachers.
Teachers' conduct is still bound by other laws and their contracts, and they should have ethical rules.
Under Article 34 of the Educational Personnel Employment Act, full-time teachers may not teach or work elsewhere unless other laws provide otherwise.

who: Teachers who also hold school administrative posts

raw.answer: The case asked whether a court precedent was unconstitutional for barring any appeal when a personnel authority found a civil servant's proposed appointment unqualified or lowered its rank. The court held that such people may seek relief through administrative appeal or administrative litigation after going through the statutory review process. The part of the precedent that conflicts with this can no longer be used.
raw.held: Civil servants whose proposed appointment is found unqualified or given a lower rank, and who still disagree after the legal review process, may file an administrative appeal or lawsuit. The conflicting part of Administrative Court precedent No. 400 (1970) is no longer to be applied.

points.text: Whether a civil servant can challenge a measure in an administrative proceeding depends on what the measure does; earlier interpretations already allowed court challenges for measures that change civil servant status or seriously affect the person.
A finding of unqualified or a lowered rank in appointment review seriously affects the constitutionally protected right to hold public office.
So after applying for review under the legal procedure and still disagreeing with the decision, the person may file an administrative appeal or lawsuit to seek relief.

The precedent said such decisions are not administrative actions toward citizens and allowed only a request for review within the agency, with no appeal; the part conflicting with this reasoning is no longer applied.
The petition on one provision of the implementing rules for reservists' transfer to public office was not accepted because no final court judgment existed.

who: Civil servants whose proposed appointment is rejected or lowered in rank

raw.answer: The case asked whether Article 330 of the Civil Code and Article 7 of the Enforcement Rules of the Deposit Act are unconstitutional. Article 330 ends a creditor's rights in deposited property after ten years of not exercising them, and the property then goes to the national treasury. The rules start the ten years the day after the deposit. The court held they are not unconstitutional, but said creditors must be properly notified, and it called for the rules to be reviewed and revised.
raw.held: The ten-year period and its start date do not conflict with the Constitution. Because forfeiture affects property rights, the depositor or the deposit office must notify the creditor by notice, service or public announcement, and if that was not done, make up the service or announcement within a reasonable time before the period ends. The enforcement rules must be thoroughly reviewed and revised.

points.text: After a deposit, the creditor can collect at any time. If the creditor does not, the deposit office must keep the property indefinitely and rights stay uncertain, which harms the economy and society.
The rules aim to settle rights in the deposited property early, which is needed to keep social order stable, so they do not conflict with the Constitution.
The law already requires the depositor to notify the creditor, and requires the deposit office to serve or announce the deposit notice.

Because the property goes to the national treasury and affects the creditor's property rights, the deposit must be notified, and if that was not done, service or announcement must be made up before the period ends.
If the property went to the treasury without such make-up notice, the creditor may still seek state compensation where the State Compensation Act's conditions are met.
The enforcement rules should be thoroughly reviewed and revised in line with this reasoning to protect people's property rights.

raw.answer: The case asked whether a constitutional interpretation body can review how the Legislative Yuan passed the laws setting up the National Security Council, National Security Bureau and Personnel Administration Bureau. The court said that how the legislature follows its own procedures is generally its internal matter, and the court reviews it only for obvious, serious constitutional defects. Because it is disputed whether these three laws were actually voted on and that cannot be shown without investigation, the Legislative Yuan must decide that itself.
raw.held: Procedures inside the legislature are generally for the legislature to decide, and a law it has sent to the President and that was promulgated takes effect. The court can strike down a law only for an obvious, serious defect in how it was made. For the three organizational laws, the Legislative Yuan must settle within a reasonable time whether they were passed and, if its result differs, send the law to the President again.

points.text: Under the separation of powers, a legislature's way of following its own rules is an internal matter that other state organs should respect, known as parliamentary self-discipline.

The Legislative Yuan has the same self-discipline power as other democratic parliaments. Its rules come from its organic act, rules of procedure and practice, and foreign court examples show respect for this.
A law promulgated by the President after the Legislative Yuan sent it over exists formally and takes effect even if it departed from the legislature's procedures.
A law can be struck down for procedural defects only if they are obvious and serious without needing fact investigation, such as skipping the required vote.

Where it is disputed whether a defect is serious and facts need investigating, the court is limited. Oral argument covers only legal questions, and summoning legislators would move a political dispute to the judiciary.

The minutes of these three laws were unconfirmed, but that did not touch the basic rules for making a law. Whether they were actually voted on is disputed and unclear, so the Legislative Yuan must resolve it in a reasonable time.

who: National Security Council, National Security Bureau and Personnel Administration Bureau

raw.answer: The case asked whether the Income Tax Act rules requiring a taxpayer to file a combined income tax return with a spouse and other dependents who have income are unconstitutional. The court found the filing requirement is not unconstitutional as a matter of procedure. But it said that if combining incomes makes a taxpayer pay more tax than filing separately, that does not fit the principle of tax fairness.
raw.held: The combined-filing rules (Articles 15 and 17, paragraph 1, of the Income Tax Act as amended in 1963) do not conflict with the Constitution as to the filing procedure. However, if combined calculation raises a household's tax compared with separate calculation, that is inconsistent with tax fairness, and the authorities should keep reviewing and improving the rules.

points.text: The combined-filing rule aims to reduce the number of returns and cases, saving effort and cost for both taxpayers and tax authorities.
As a filing procedure, combined filing is necessary to advance the public interest, so it does not conflict with the Constitution.
If combined calculation of tax is higher than separate calculation, it does not fit the principle of tax fairness.

Although the rules were partly amended on 30 December 1989, the responsible authority should keep weighing related laws and social and economic conditions and improve them, including the exemption and deduction rules.

who: Taxpayers who file with a spouse who has income
Taxpayers who file with other dependents who have income

raw.answer: The case asked what "continuing service" means in Article 6 of the School Staff Retirement Act, which gives extra retirement pay to teachers or principals with 30 years of service and 20 years of continuous service. The court ruled that it means the job held at retirement must connect directly, without a gap, to the 20 years of continuous service as a teacher or principal.
raw.held: "Continuing service" in Article 6 means that the teacher's or principal's position at retirement links up without any break to their 20 years of continuous service.

points.text: Ordinary public servants reach the maximum retirement pay (61 base units for a lump sum) at 30 years, so more service adds nothing. Article 6 adds extra units for teachers and principals who keep serving, up to 81 in total.
The extra pay aims to encourage teachers and principals to stay in their jobs with dedication for a long time.
It also aims to stop other people from moving into teaching or principal posts shortly before retiring just to get better retirement pay.

The statute puts "excellent record and still continuing service" right after "20 years of continuous service", which shows this purpose, so the service must connect to that 20-year record without a gap.

Whether someone who served 20 years, moved to school inspector or other specialist education administration, and later returned to teaching or as principal should be covered is a matter for lawmakers, not decided here.

raw.answer: The case asked whether a rule in the Customs Act (as amended on 29 June 1986) is unconstitutional. The rule required importers who disputed a customs assessment to pay the full tax, or provide adequate security, within a deadline, or lose the chance to seek review. The court decided that this rule unnecessarily limits people's right to bring legal action and conflicts with Article 16 of the Constitution.
raw.held: Article 23 of the Customs Act, as amended on 29 June 1986, takes away administrative remedies from taxpayers who cannot pay the assessed tax in full or provide adequate security in time. This is an unnecessary restriction on the right to sue and conflicts with Article 16 of the Constitution.

points.text: The court had already said in earlier interpretations (Nos. 224 and 288) that making a tax review conditional on paying a set share of the tax or providing security is an unnecessary limit on appeal and litigation rights, and is inconsistent with Article 16.
Article 23 required the full tax to be paid, or security provided, within 14 days to request review, and treated a taxpayer who did not do so as not having requested review.

The rule aimed to stop people from requesting review at will to delay paying tax, but under the existing system, bringing an administrative remedy does not stop the original decision from being enforced.

As a result, the rule only costs taxpayers who cannot pay in full or give adequate security in time their chance at an administrative remedy, which is an unnecessary restriction on the right to sue under Article 16.

who: Importers and taxpayers disputing customs assessments
Taxpayers unable to pay in full or provide security

raw.answer: Someone asked the Constitutional Court to interpret what the "inherent territory" of the Republic of China means under Article 4 of the Constitution. The court declined to interpret it. It said that defining the national territory is a major political question that a court should not decide.
raw.held: The court held that defining the scope of the "inherent territory" in Article 4 is a major political question and should not be interpreted by the constitutional interpretation body, so the request was not interpreted.

points.text: Article 4 does not list the territory. It uses a general phrase, "according to its inherent territory," and sets a procedure for changing territory as a limit, for political and historical reasons.
How national territory is defined is purely a political question. Doctrine calls such acts "acts of state" (統治行為), which under the separation of powers are not subject to judicial review.
Explaining what "inherent territory" means would necessarily involve defining the territory's scope, which is a major political question.
For these reasons, the request should not be interpreted.

who: Those who petitioned for the interpretation

raw.answer: The case asked whether a provision of the Income Tax Act that fines withholding agents who fail to file or issue withholding certificates on time is unconstitutional. The court held that the penalty provision does not conflict with the Constitution, because it serves the public interest. But it said the fixed-percentage fine with no reasonable cap can be too harsh when the tax was paid on time, so the relevant authorities should review and fix it.
raw.held: Article 114, item 2, first part of the Income Tax Act is not in conflict with the Constitution as far as it punishes breaching the duty to file or issue certificates on time. However, fining a fixed percentage of the tax with no reasonable maximum, where the tax was paid to the treasury on time and only the filing or issuing was late, should be reviewed and revised by the relevant authorities.

points.text: The provision punishes withholding agents who do not file or issue withholding certificates within the legal deadline.
The penalty aims to enforce the withholding system and push agents to do their duty, so tax authorities can get tax-source data, keep taxation fair and secure state revenue.
It is a necessary means and not a pointless burden on agents, so the sanction for breaching this duty serves the public interest and does not conflict with the Constitution.
Where the agent paid the withheld tax to the treasury on time and was only late in filing or issuing, a fine at a fixed percentage of the tax with no reasonable maximum may be excessive.
The relevant authorities should therefore review and revise this part.

who: Agents who paid on time but filed or issued late

raw.answer: The case asked whether it is unconstitutional to require a defense lawyer from the original trial to file an appeal in the defendant's name, and to refuse any fixing of the paperwork if that is missing. The court held that requiring the defendant's name does not violate the constitutional right to sue. But if the lawyer filed for the defendant's benefit and only left out the defendant's name, the court must first set a deadline to fix it, and a dismissal without that step must be remedied under the law.
raw.held: The rule that a trial defense lawyer must appeal in the defendant's name does not conflict with the constitutional protection of litigation rights. However, a missing 'in the defendant's name' statement can be corrected, so a court that dismissed the appeal without first ordering a correction must be given legal remedy. Supreme Court precedent No. 20 (1980), which treated the defect as uncorrectable, is not to be applied.

points.text: The appeal by a trial defense lawyer is not independent, so it must be made in the defendant's name. This does not restrict the defendant's right to appeal and saves cost and delay, so it does not conflict with the constitutional right to sue.
An appeal filed this way is the lawyer's act, not the defendant's, and the defendant cannot be expected to notice whether the filing says it is in their name.

The earlier precedent itself called the omission a procedural defect, and the lawyer who filed can fix it. Under the cited provisions, the court or presiding judge should set a deadline and first order a correction.

This protects the defendant from unexpected harm to the right to appeal caused by the lawyer's carelessness about procedure. If the appeal was dismissed without ordering a correction first, it must be remedied under the law.
The 1980 Supreme Court precedent said the defect could not be corrected, which is inconsistent with this reasoning, so it should not be applied.

who: Defense lawyers from the original trial

raw.answer: The case asked whether a Ministry of Finance circular was unconstitutional for making businesses pay back taxes and penalties for tax evasion even when they had not falsely reported input tax. The court held that the business tax law's penalty applies only when a business falsely reported input tax and thereby evaded tax. To the extent the circular went beyond that, it violated the constitution's protection of people's rights and may no longer be applied.
raw.held: The Ministry of Finance's 1987 circular, to the extent it penalized businesses that had real purchases under the business tax law's provision whether or not they falsely reported input tax and evaded tax, goes against the constitution and must no longer be applied. The penalty standards in the provision themselves are within the legislature's discretion and are constitutional.

points.text: Article 51 of the business tax law punishes tax evasion, so punishing false reporting of input tax requires both the false reporting and an actual loss of tax.
This differs from Article 44 of the Tax Collection Act, which punishes merely failing to give or obtain receipts, whether or not there was false reporting and evasion.

The circular did not state this meaning and punished businesses with real purchases regardless of false reporting or evasion, so the inconsistent part violates the constitution's protection of rights.
The Article 51 penalties aim to prevent evasion and achieve correct taxation, so the penalty standards stay within the legislature's discretion and do not conflict with the constitution.
Punishing a buyer who fails to obtain a receipt from the direct seller under Article 44 is consistent with an earlier interpretation (No. 252) on sellers not issuing receipts.
Penalties for such conduct and for evasion differ in purpose and requirements; whether both may be imposed together is a matter of applying the law and legislation.

who: Ministry of Finance and tax authorities

raw.answer: The case asked whether a rule in the Educational Personnel Employment Act barring teachers who have been suspended from duty over a case from working as educators is unconstitutional. The court held that the rule is not unconstitutional, because suspended people are not suited to keep doing educational work for the time being. It also said that a suspended teacher who is later cleared and rehired should have the rights lost in the gap addressed, and the competent authority should review how.
raw.held: Article 31, item 3 of the Educational Personnel Employment Act, which bars people whose suspension from duty over a case has not ended from being educators, does not conflict with the Constitution. The competent authority should review how to compensate for rights lost by suspended teachers who are later cleared by legal process and rehired by their original school after their term ended.

points.text: Teachers under suspension have difficulty concentrating on their work, which could disrupt the normal running of education, so they are temporarily unsuited to continue in educational duties.
Because of this, the rule is necessary to advance the public interest and does not conflict with the Constitution.

Where schools use a contract system, a suspended teacher who is cleared of criminal and administrative liability and rehired shows the matter was resolved, yet current law has no rule on compensating rights lost between the end of the old term and the rehiring.
This gap in the law is an omission, so the competent authority should review and handle it.

The enforcement rule requiring written notice a month before a term ends when a school will not renew a teacher only sets a procedure to make schools handle non-renewal carefully, and the court's earlier Interpretation No. 203 already found it not unconstitutional.
How that rule is applied is not a matter of constitutional interpretation.

who: Teachers suspended from duty over a case
Schools that hire teachers on contracts

raw.answer: The case asked whether a 1990 Ministry of Education circular was unconstitutional. The circular let people who had worked as childcare-centre (托兒所) staff count that service toward a pay raise when moving to a public kindergarten teaching job, but only if they already held kindergarten teacher qualifications at the time. The court decided that limiting the pay-raise credit this way does not conflict with the Constitution.
raw.held: The court held that the Ministry's circular, which credits past childcare-centre service for pay-step raises only where the person already qualified as a kindergarten teacher at the time, does not conflict with the Constitution.

points.text: Childcare centres and kindergartens both concern young children's healthy development, but kindergartens must also provide pre-school health, daily-life and ethics education, so their tasks differ from those of childcare centres.
Kindergarten teacher qualifications are set out expressly in Article 12 of the Kindergarten Education Act, promulgated on 6 November 1981.
So public childcare-centre staff can have their years of service counted for a pay raise when moving to a public kindergarten only if they held the legally required qualifications.
The Ministry's 1990 circular, which allows one pay step per full year of service, capped at the highest pay of the post, matches this reasoning and so does not conflict with the Constitution.

who: Former childcare-centre staff moving to public kindergartens
Childcare-centre staff without kindergarten teacher qualifications

raw.answer: The Legislative Yuan and the Executive Yuan disagreed over what "public bonds" means in Article 2 of the Central Government Construction Bond Issuance Act, and the Legislative Yuan asked the court to settle it. The court said the Act's term covers only construction bonds issued as bond certificates under the law. It also said that, in the broad sense, public debt includes all government borrowing, and that a ceiling on total national borrowing should be set by law.
raw.held: In the broad sense, public debt means all public debts including government borrowing. The "public bonds" in the Construction Bond Issuance Act means only construction bonds issued as bond certificates under the law. To keep national finances sound, a ceiling on total national borrowing should be set by law after overall consideration.

points.text: The Legislative Yuan's request met the legal requirements, and the court accepted it after hearing both bodies and inviting finance scholars to speak.

Broadly, public debt covers government borrowing from individuals, groups, financial institutions, foreign governments or international organizations on a promise to repay principal and interest. In the narrow sense it means raising money by issuing bond certificates.

The Construction Bond Act deals only with bonds or certificates issued to raise construction funds. Its "outstanding total balance" therefore covers only such bonds, not short-term notes issued under other laws or bank loans of over a year.
Borrowing and bond issuance are both public debt and in substance the same kind of financing tool. Other government borrowing is bound by specific laws with maximum amounts or budget-based limits.

Loans of over one year are only put in the annual budget for the Legislative Yuan to review, and no law caps them. This makes the Act's ceiling an empty rule, is unbalanced compared with other borrowing, and invites avoiding the limit.
So, to protect sound national finances, a ceiling on total national borrowing should be set by law.

raw.answer: The case asked whether rules issued by the Ministry of Education for publicly funded students at National Yang-Ming Medical College were unconstitutional. The rules require graduates to serve in public health institutions after graduation, and their professional certificates are held by the assigning agency until service ends. The court found the rules do not conflict with the Constitution.
raw.held: The Yang-Ming publicly funded medical student rules, including points 13 and 14 on post-graduation assignment and certificate custody, do not conflict with the Constitution. Any limits on students' rights come from the contract they entered, not from the rules themselves.

points.text: Administrative agencies may, within their legal powers and without breaking the law, agree to provide a benefit and require the recipient to accept reasonable burdens or public-law duties, creating an administrative contract.
The rules were made to solve the difficulty of filling doctor vacancies in public medical institutions by training people through publicly funded medical education.

Points 13 and 14 (certificate custody by the assigning agency, no issuance of certificates before service ends, and repayment of costs for those who do not serve) ensure that students who chose public funding serve as agreed. This is necessary for the administrative goal and does not go beyond a reasonable scope.

The rules serve as the basis for contracts with students who voluntarily accept publicly funded education, and once a contract (such as a written statement of intent or guarantee) is made, they become its terms, which both sides must perform in good faith.
So any limit on students' rights results from being bound by the contract, not from the rules themselves, and the rules do not conflict with the Constitution.

who: Publicly funded medical students at National Yang-Ming Medical College
Graduates assigned to public health institutions
Ministry of Education and assigning agencies

raw.answer: The case asked whether Article 866 of the Civil Code and an earlier court interpretation (院字第1446號) are unconstitutional. The article and the interpretation say that rights set up on a property after a mortgage cannot harm the mortgage. The court decided they do not conflict with the Constitution.
raw.held: Article 866 of the Civil Code and interpretation 院字第1446號 do not conflict with the Constitution. A later right that does not affect the mortgage may continue to exist.

points.text: A mortgage is a property right, and registering it makes it publicly known. So anyone who gets a superficies right (地上權) or other right to use the property after registration cannot let that right harm the earlier mortgage.

If a later right affects the mortgage and the property is auctioned with no buyer or too low a bid to repay the debt, the right must be removed for the auction. The holder's possession is then ended and the property handed over to the buyer. This is needed so the mortgagee is repaid based on the property's condition when the mortgage was created.
If the later right does not affect the mortgage, it may continue to exist, so the interests of those who acquired rights later are also taken into account.
So the proviso of Article 866 and interpretation 院字第1446號 do not conflict with the Constitution's protection of people's rights.

who: Property owners who set up mortgages
People who later get land-use rights on mortgaged property

raw.answer: The case asked whether a rule in Taiwan's criminal procedure law is unconstitutional because it allows an appeal to the third-instance court only on the ground that the judgment violated the law. The court decided the rule is constitutional. It said the rule is meant to make reasonable use of court procedures and serves the public interest.
raw.held: Article 377 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which allows a third-instance appeal only on the ground that the judgment violated the law, stays within the legislature's discretion and does not conflict with Article 16 of the Constitution.

points.text: Article 16 of the Constitution gives people the right to bring lawsuits, but how that right is exercised, how court levels are divided, and whether the third-instance court is a court of law only are matters for the legislature to set by statute.
Limiting third-instance appeals to judgments that violate the law is meant to make use of court procedures reasonable and to advance the public interest.

The limit is necessary for the public interest and does not exceed the legislature's discretion. Article 23 of the Constitution permits it, so it does not conflict with the protection of the right to sue in Article 16.

who: Criminal defendants wanting a third-instance appeal

raw.answer: The case asked whether a Ministry of Finance letter violated the Constitution by refusing to let people pay inheritance tax with privately built road land. The court decided the letter does not conflict with the Constitution. It reasoned that such land is hard to sell for cash, so it is not suitable for paying the tax.
raw.held: The Ministry of Finance's 1982 letter, which bars land that became a road in use but was not designated as planned road land under urban planning and was built by private persons from being used to pay inheritance tax, does not conflict with the Constitution.

points.text: Under the Estate and Gift Tax Act article 30, paragraph 2, inheritance tax is meant to be paid in cash; paying with property is allowed only when cash payment is truly difficult.
The tax authority must investigate and decide whether that condition is met and whether the property is suitable for payment. Taxpayers cannot pick any property they like.

Paying with property is meant to be turned into cash, so the enforcement rules require property that is easy to sell or keep and has no other rights set on it. Being easy to sell is not optional just because it is listed alongside safekeeping.
Accepting property that cannot be sold would only burden the state with pointless storage, which goes against the purpose of the Act.

Privately built road land not designated as planned road land under urban planning gives the authorities no duty to expropriate it, so it is hard to sell. There is therefore no reason to let it pay the tax.
The rules and the letter are needed to carry out the tax law and to encourage honest tax paying, so they do not conflict with the Constitution.

who: Owners of privately built road land

raw.answer: The case asked whether Taiwan's rules for valuing an estate when the heirs file the estate tax return late, and the penalty for late filing, are unconstitutional. The court said the rule that uses a higher later market value, placed alongside the separate fine, risks punishing the same conduct twice and should be reviewed and revised quickly. It found that charging interest on late-paid tax does not conflict with the Constitution.
raw.held: The rule letting a higher later-date value replace the value at death for late filers, combined with the Article 44 fine, risks double punishment and must be reviewed and fixed promptly. Adding interest to back taxes under Tax Collection Act Article 48-1, paragraph 1 proviso, is not unconstitutional.

points.text: Inheritance begins at the death, and heirs take over the deceased's rights and duties then, so the estate tax duty arises at that moment. This is why estate value is normally counted at the market value on the date of death.
The higher-value rule for late filers aims to stop taxpayers from being opportunistic and waiting to see how values move.

But that rule counts value gained after the heirs already acquired the estate, and it sits alongside the fine of one to two times the tax for failing to file on time, with no rule to apply only one. This risks repeated punishment.
Land inherited and later transferred is taxed on its value increase using the announced value at the start of inheritance, so related laws need to be coordinated and quickly reviewed and revised.
Interest on back taxes is added because a taxpayer who pays late gains a benefit from holding the money, so this does not conflict with the Constitution.

who: Heirs who file estate tax late
Heirs who inherit and later sell land

raw.answer: The case asked whether the Company Act's rule that a company's registration changes be filed by the company's responsible person is unconstitutional. The court decided it is not, because a company is a legal person that must act through its representative, and this protects transaction security.
raw.held: The Company Act Article 403, paragraph 1 requires changes to registered matters to be applied for within fifteen days. Under paragraph 2, the company's responsible person must file, and this does not conflict with the Constitution.

points.text: A company is an independent holder of rights and duties, so changes to its organization, capital and similar matters must be recorded by the proper legal procedure in the authority's registers, open for public viewing and copying.
Because a company is a legal person, its representative must be the one to apply for the change registration, as the ruling reads Article 403, paragraph 2 and Article 387.
Having the representative apply helps ensure the safety of transactions, so the rule does not conflict with the Constitution.
If a responsible person files false registration details, whether they face criminal liability under Article 9, paragraph 2 of the Company Act is a separate question.

who: Members of the public who consult company registers

raw.answer: The case asked whether a rule limiting what exam takers can demand when they ask for a recheck of their exam scores is unconstitutional. The rule, Article 8 of the Examination Yuan's 1986 measures on handling score rechecks, bars requests for regrading, model answers, viewing or copying papers, and graders' names. The court held the rule does not conflict with the Constitution, but said recheck matters should preferably be set by statute.
raw.held: Once exam papers are unsealed, they should not be arbitrarily regraded at an exam taker's request, unless an obvious error is visible on the face of the paper. Article 8 of the recheck measures is necessary and consistent with the Constitution, though recheck matters should preferably be set by law.

points.text: Exams are run by an exam committee under the watch of supervising Control Yuan members, who handle any cheating, so the process has built-in safeguards.

Graders score papers while they are sealed. Regrading after unsealing at an applicant's request would be hard to keep objective and fair, since a prior score exists and the grader might learn who the applicant is, even if the paper were resealed.
Article 8 is needed to protect the exam's objectivity and fairness and to respect graders' academic judgment.
Article 8 matches the Examination Personnel Act's Article 23 requirement that exam staff keep secrecy.
Obvious errors such as a missed paper can still be fixed under Article 7 of the measures.
Because rechecks serve exam takers' interests, recheck matters should preferably be set by law.

who: Exam takers seeking a score recheck

raw.answer: The case asked whether the legal basis for penalties in the civil air transport business management rules was constitutional. The court found that the legal authorization behind fining airlines for carrying passengers without an entry visa or permit was not clear enough. That part of the penalty provisions will lose effect within one year at the latest.
raw.held: The part of the rules that punishes violations of Article 29, paragraph 1 by applying Article 87, item 7 of the Civil Aviation Act has an unclear legal basis and conflicts with the constitutional principle. It will lose effect from the announcement date, at the latest when one year has passed.

points.text: Fines for breaking administrative duties restrict people's rights, so the elements of the offense and the amount must be set by law.

If a law lets an order fill in the elements of an offense, the content and scope of that authorization must be specific and clear, and the order must be issued on that basis, in line with Article 23 of the Constitution.

Article 29, paragraph 1 bars airlines from carrying passengers without a Republic of China entry visa or permit. The transport ministry added it in a September 1988 amendment, in response to needs after martial law ended.
Although the rules were made under Article 92 of the Civil Aviation Act, the legal authorization for punishing violations of that provision through Article 46 and Article 87, item 7 is unclear.
Article 87, item 7 fines any other violation of the Act or of orders issued under it. The court called this a vague authorization with no fixed scope and said it should also be reviewed.

who: Airlines fined for carrying passengers without entry papers
Authorities that make and apply aviation penalty rules

raw.answer: The case asked whether earlier court precedents barring civil servants from challenging the pay grade (級俸) set for them were unconstitutional. The court decided that civil servants who dispute their approved pay grade may file an administrative appeal and an administrative lawsuit. The two precedents that said otherwise may no longer be used.
raw.held: A civil servant who disputes the pay grade assigned to them may bring an administrative appeal and an administrative lawsuit, following the same reasoning as Interpretation No. 323. The two Administrative Court precedents (Nos. 414 of year 57 and 400 of year 59) are no longer to be applied, and Interpretation No. 323 is supplemented.

points.text: Whether a civil servant can appeal or sue over an administrative action affecting their status depends on what the action contains, as earlier interpretations explained.

Under Interpretation No. 323, when an agency finds a person unqualified or lowers the rank first intended for them, this greatly affects the constitutionally protected right to hold public office, so they may appeal and sue.
Because the same reasoning applies, a dispute over the approved pay grade also allows an administrative appeal and lawsuit.
As a result, the two earlier Administrative Court precedents should no longer be applied, and Interpretation No. 323 is supplemented.

who: Public employees whose qualifications are reviewed
Agencies that review and set pay grades

raw.answer: The case asked whether rules for a 1990 special civil service exam for Taiwan Province grassroots staff were unconstitutional. The rules sorted candidates by region for registration, admission and posting, and required those hired to serve in their original region for a set period. The court decided the rules do not conflict with the constitutional guarantee of equality.
raw.held: Article 3 of the 1990 exam rules (regional registration, admission and assignment, plus a required period of service in the original region) was set by the Examination Yuan within its powers and does not violate the equality right in Article 7 of the Constitution.

points.text: The Examination Yuan is the highest exam body and may make exam rules under its legal powers, so long as it does not exceed those powers or infringe people's right to take exams, as an earlier interpretation (No. 155) said.

Equality under Article 7, and in the right to take exams under Article 18, means substantive equality, so reasonable limits made for real needs and the exam's purpose do not breach it, as an earlier interpretation (No. 205) said.
The regional system and required service period were necessary measures responding to grassroots agencies' staffing needs and candidates' preferences.
This is comparable to authorities holding separate special exams in each county or city for local agencies and public enterprises at the same time.
The exam committee may set pass marks for each region and category based on reported vacancies and scores, so pass marks naturally differ between regions, which candidates could foresee.

who: Candidates for the 1990 Taiwan Province grassroots special exam
Exam passers required to serve in their original region
Grassroots agencies and public enterprises below provincial level
Examination Yuan and the exam committee

raw.answer: The case asked whether it is unconstitutional that the election and recall law does not allow recall of overseas-citizen and nationwide at-large (not district-based) legislators. The court decided the rule does not conflict with the Constitution, because these members are chosen by party vote share rather than directly by district voters. It also said that a member who loses membership in the party that put them in office should lose their seat, with replacements to be set by law.
raw.held: The provision exempting nationwide at-large and overseas-citizen winners from recall does not conflict with the Constitution. A member who loses the membership of the party they were elected through should lose their central representative seat, and how vacancies are filled must be set by law.

points.text: Under the constitutional amendment, overseas-citizen and at-large seats are filled by party vote share, not by direct votes in an electoral district.
Because district voters did not directly elect them, those voters cannot recall them by vote; this limits the public's recall right, and the law's exemption follows from that.
These seats were created so some representatives are not limited by local interests and can look to the national interest, with parties choosing respected members.
Since the member won through the party's share of votes, losing party membership removes the basis of their election, so they should lose their seat, in line with the purpose of the system.
Filling the resulting vacancy should be decided by law, to keep party politics working normally.

raw.answer: The case asked whether a Ministry of Finance rule on managing cargo containers is unconstitutional. The rule lets customs stop accepting a container depot's applications to bring in goods for a period of time when goods go missing from the depot. The court held that customs may do this because it is needed for the public interest, but the period has no maximum length, so a law or a law-authorized order must set limits by the end of 1994 or the rule stops applying.
raw.held: Article 26 (first part) of the Customs Container Management Rules is acceptable in letting customs suspend a depot's intake applications for a set period after goods go missing. However, the period has no maximum, so a law or law-authorized order must set it by December 31, 1994, or the suspension rule stops applying.

points.text: Depots are licensed and registered with customs, and their work is closely tied to customs inspection and anti-smuggling duties, which is why the Finance Ministry made rules making depots responsible for stored goods.
When stored goods go missing, smuggling or other illegal acts may occur, so customs may suspend intake to protect its monitoring of stored goods and prevent smuggling.
Suspension pushes depots to improve their facilities or management and stops harm from continuing or growing, so it serves the public interest and fits customs' legal duties.
The rule sets no maximum length for the suspension, so the period must be set by a law or law-authorized order, drawing on Article 63 of the Shipping Act, to match Article 23 of the Constitution.

Because depot operators must give customs a written guarantee, public-law contract issues arise, and the relevant bodies should promptly legislate basic rules for them, in line with administration according to law.
The part making the depot pay import duties needs no new interpretation, since the depot is the holder when the shortage occurs and Interpretation No. 219 applies.

who: Importers whose goods are stored in depots

raw.answer: The case asked whether a Ministry of Examination circular was unconstitutional for refusing medical payments to a civil servant who was in a vegetative state, on the ground that complications from the disability could not be treated to an end. The court found that the circular treated disability benefits and illness or injury benefits as one insured event, added a condition the law does not contain, and did not fit the constitutional aim of social insurance. It ruled the circular should no longer be applied.
raw.held: The circular of 6 October 1990 is inconsistent with the constitution's purpose of social insurance protecting people with disabilities and should no longer be applied. The insurer must still cover treatment for illnesses or injuries other than the brain condition after disability benefits are paid.

points.text: Civil servant insurance is social insurance, and the constitution (Article 155) requires the state to give suitable help to people who are disabled and cannot support themselves, so the right to disability benefits touches constitutional rights.
The insurance law lists illness, injury and disability as separate insured events, so a disability that has occurred must be paid as disability under Article 14 and the implementing rules.

The rule barring renewed treatment for the same illness or injury after disability payment is a separate question about illness or injury benefits and has nothing to do with whether disability benefits are owed.

The implementing rules define the same illness or injury by an enumerated list and do not include infections and complications that are not the same illness or injury; conditions that could arise in non-disabled people cannot be stretched into the same event.

The circular accepted that the brain condition could end treatment, which meets the disability condition, but then refused payment because complications could not end treatment. This mixed up the two insured events and added a condition the law lacks.

Specialized care beyond treatment matters more than the disability payment, and the current insurance lacks rules for it, so this should be reviewed quickly. Treatment for other illnesses or injuries unrelated to the brain condition must still be paid by the insurer.

who: People with disabilities receiving disability benefits
Insurance carrier and Ministry of Examination

raw.answer: The case asked whether a Supreme Court precedent is unconstitutional. That precedent says an agreement among co-owners to divide or share use of property still binds someone who later buys a co-owner's share. The court held that the precedent conflicts with the constitutional protection of property when the buyer did not know, and could not have known, about the agreement, so it should no longer be applied in that situation.
raw.held: The precedent should no longer be applied where the buyer of a co-owner's share did not know and could not have known of the sharing or division agreement. The court also said legislation should be passed quickly on how the legally required open space of buildings with divided ownership is used and transferred.

points.text: Under civil law, a contract (a creditor-debtor act) normally binds only the specific parties, while a property act made public through a recognized method affects everyone.
Movables are made public by delivery and real estate by registration, which protects good-faith third parties.
If a third party knew or could have known the facts, even a contract's terms can still have legal effect on that party.
The precedent is considered necessary to keep the legal order stable.
But binding a buyer who neither knew nor could have known of the agreement risks unexpected harm to an innocent third party, which conflicts with constitutional property protection.
The court asked for quick legislation on use and transfer of the legal open space in buildings with divided ownership, including whether it is shared or exclusively used.

who: Buyers of a co-owner's share in property
Co-owners who made division or sharing agreements
Owners in buildings with divided ownership

raw.answer: The case asked what 'river channel' (河道) means in the Urban Planning Act, and whether an existing 'flood-way zone' (行水區) counts. The court decided that a river channel means one deliberately planned and built under urban planning. Naturally formed rivers and the original flood-way zones officially declared under the Water Act are not included, even if they lie inside an urban planning area.
raw.held: The river channel referred to in Article 42, paragraph 1, item 1 of the Urban Planning Act means a channel set up through reasonable planning under Article 3 of that Act. Naturally formed rivers, and original flood-way zones declared under the Water Act because of them, are not included even when inside an urban planning use zone.

points.text: Urban planning means planning important facilities for urban life and making reasonable plans for land use, as Article 3 of the Urban Planning Act states.
The river channel in Article 42 is one reasonably planned and set up under that rule, and one that should first use suitable publicly owned land under the article's second paragraph.
Such a channel's land was not a river channel originally; it became a public facility site only through the urban plan.
Naturally formed rivers and original flood-way zones declared under the Water Act were not set up under the Urban Planning Act, so they are not public facility sites, even if renamed river channels.
Use zones or special-purpose zones under Article 32 exist to regulate land use, which is different from setting up public facility sites.

who: Owners and users of land in urban planning areas
Authorities handling urban planning and water management

raw.answer: The case asked whether Taiwan's Bankruptcy Act is unconstitutional because it lets a court keep extending the detention of a bankrupt person with no limit on the number of extensions. The court said detention itself is justified to protect the bankruptcy estate, but the lack of any limit on extensions conflicts with the constitutional protection of personal liberty. The law must be amended quickly, and the unlimited-extension part stops applying one year after the ruling is published.
raw.held: The part of Article 71, paragraph 2 of the Bankruptcy Act that lets detention be extended without suitable limits on the number of extensions is inconsistent with the constitution's protection of personal freedom. It must be amended promptly and stops being applied at the latest one year after the ruling is published; until then courts must apply it carefully in light of the ruling.

points.text: Detention of a bankrupt person who may flee or hide or destroy property is accepted as necessary to protect the estate, safeguard all creditors, and let the bankruptcy proceeding finish.
Apart from people finally sentenced to life imprisonment for a crime, restrictions on personal freedom under current law all have time limits.

Compared with enforcement law, which caps custody at three months and allows only one re-custody for a new cause, and with criminal procedure law, which limits detention periods and extensions, the bankruptcy rule has no limit on extensions.
Because bankruptcy detention mainly aims to protect the estate, unlimited extensions are clearly inappropriate, easy to abuse, and against the constitution's protection of personal freedom.

The legislature should review the whole matter, including the name 'detention', the limits on extensions or total period, and how to supervise a bankrupt person who is not physically held and punish breaches.
A bankrupt person suspected of the crimes in Articles 152 to 159 should be sent to prosecutors, who may detain them under the law if necessary; this is a separate issue.

raw.answer: The case asked whether a rule in the implementing regulations of the law on handling soldier land-grant certificates was unconstitutional. The rule paid the disability-level compensation only if the war injury happened on or after October 18, 1951. The court found the rule inconsistent with the law and harmful to people's protected rights, and said it must not be applied.
raw.held: The regulation's rule limiting disability-level compensation to injuries after October 18, 1951 does not match the law and goes against the constitution's protection of people's rights, so it must not be applied. The competent authority must decide which battles count as the cause of the injury, in line with the purpose of the two laws.

points.text: The law on handling the certificates was made to take back land-grant certificates already issued, giving different numbers of compensation units depending on the person's situation.

The original land-grant law took effect on October 18, 1951, but its Articles 5 and 11(2) show that whether someone was disabled when certificates were issued did not depend on the injury happening after that date.

The handling law deals with existing facts, namely certificates already issued or treated as issued, so there is no issue of retroactive effect, and it does not limit disability to injuries after that date.

The regulation's Article 3(3) limited disability status to injuries after October 18, 1951, so people injured earlier who held certificates lost the chance to receive disability-level compensation, which conflicts with the law and with constitutional protection of rights.
Which battles count as the cause of the injury is for the competent authority to define, considering the land-grant law's definition of soldier and the total compensation limit in the handling law.

who: Certificate holders injured in battle before October 18, 1951
The competent authority that defines the qualifying battles

raw.answer: The case was about what route a retired civil servant can use to challenge a dispute over a welfare mutual-aid payment. The court decided that claiming this payment under the rules is a public-law property claim. If the claim is refused, the person may use an administrative appeal or an administrative lawsuit.
raw.held: Civil servants whose public-law property claims are harmed may seek relief through administrative appeal or administrative litigation. Claiming a welfare mutual-aid payment on retirement counts as such a claim, and Interpretations No. 187, No. 201 and No. 266 are supplemented accordingly.

points.text: The constitution protects property rights, and they are not weakened because someone becomes a civil servant with a public-law service relationship to the state.

The state must protect civil servants' property rights whether they arise from public-law or private-law relationships, and there must be a legal remedy if they are harmed, so civil servants can focus on their work, in line with Article 83.
The welfare mutual-aid rules are made by the Executive Yuan or other agencies to stabilize civil servants' lives, and some involve public funds, so they are public-law in nature.

Since the court system separates civil lawsuits from administrative disputes, claiming this payment on retirement is a public-law property claim. If an agency refuses it, the person's protected property right is affected, so an administrative appeal or lawsuit must be allowed.

The earlier Administrative Court precedent that flatly barred civil servants from filing administrative appeals, regardless of the content of the decision, conflicts with this principle and should no longer be used.

raw.answer: The case asked whether two laws that let authorities collect an education levy (教育捐) were unconstitutional because they delegated the power to collect it. The court decided the delegation provisions in the National Education Act and the Revenue Allocation Act do not conflict with the Constitution.
raw.held: The court held that Article 16(1)(3) of the National Education Act and Article 18(1) of the Revenue Allocation Act, which authorize collecting the education levy, do not conflict with the Constitution.

points.text: Article 19 of the Constitution means tax duties must be set by law, but it does not limit which kind of law must set them.
A legislature may authorize an agency to decide whether to levy a tax, as long as the delegation has a specific purpose, concrete content and a clear scope.
The laws' purpose is that local tax rates are already flexible and set by local representative bodies, so no second local approval is needed when the levy is no more than 30% of the original rate.
The laws do not let the executive raise the rates the local bodies set; they only let the authority approve directly within the legal limit of 30% of the original rate.
This meets the requirements of specific purpose, concrete content and clear scope, so it does not conflict with the Constitution.
Whether to add the levy to only one of several local taxes is for the administrative agency to decide within the law, and it should consider this overall and review it from time to time.

raw.answer: The case asked whether a rule in the public office election and recall law was unconstitutional. The rule halved the candidate deposit for candidates nominated by a political party. The court decided the rule treats candidates without party backing unfairly and goes against the constitution's equality clause, so it can no longer be applied.
raw.held: The provision that lets party-nominated district and mountain-indigenous candidates pay half the deposit (but full if the party withdraws its nomination) conflicts with Article 7 of the Constitution and is no longer to be applied.

points.text: Article 7 of the Constitution says all citizens are equal before the law regardless of party.
The rule makes candidates without a party nomination pay a higher deposit than party-nominated candidates, which is an unreasonable difference in treatment.
If the announced deposit is high, people could form a party with a few others and use its nomination to cut their cost, which would produce many small parties and not help healthy party politics.
The rule is an unnecessary limit on citizens' right to take part in politics, so it does not fit Article 7 and stops applying from the day the interpretation was published.
The separate rule that a candidate's party affiliation is not printed if the candidate lacks party nomination or the party withdrew it was said not to harm constitutional rights.

who: Citizens seeking to run for office

raw.answer: The case asked whether Article 83-1 of the Income Tax Act, added in 1982, is unconstitutional. It lets tax officials investigate indirect evidence, such as net worth, flow of funds and business data that departs from normal practice, when a taxpayer is strongly suspected of major tax evasion. The court decided the article does not conflict with the Constitution.
raw.held: Article 83-1 of the Income Tax Act, as amended on 30 December 1982, is not in conflict with the Constitution. It sets out investigation methods for major suspected tax evasion cases and lets the taxpayer present counter-evidence.

points.text: The law sets out by statute how to investigate cases of major suspected tax evasion. Officials may check net worth, flow of funds and business data that departs from normal practice, with approval from the Ministry of Finance.
Tax officials may use these indirect evidence checks to calculate the taxpayer's income.
Evasion must be shown by the investigation results, judged reasonably. Only then must the taxpayer prove the facts that favor them.
The taxpayer is allowed to present counter-evidence, which protects their rights.
The provision exists only to find the truth, so it raises no problem of applying to past events.

who: Taxpayers suspected of major tax evasion
Investigators designated by the Ministry of Finance

raw.answer: The case asked whether the rules that let authorities restrict people who owe taxes, and the responsible persons of businesses that owe taxes, from leaving the country violate the Constitution. The court decided the rules do not conflict with the Constitution. It said they follow the authority given by law and are needed to secure tax revenue and serve the public interest.
raw.held: The Executive Yuan's 1984 measures restricting departure by tax debtors or heads of tax-owing businesses, including Article 2, paragraph 1, stay within the authority granted by law and do not conflict with the Constitution.

points.text: The tax collection law and the customs law expressly authorized the Executive Yuan to set implementing rules, and the 1984 measures were made under that authorization.

Article 2, paragraph 1 sets thresholds for restriction: overdue, finalized tax debts of NT$500,000 or more for individuals and NT$1,000,000 or more for businesses. It did not go beyond the purpose and scope of the authorizing laws.
Article 5 of the measures requires the restriction to be lifted immediately when any of six listed situations applies, so taxpayers' interests are taken into account.
The departure restriction is necessary to secure tax revenue and advance the public interest, so it does not conflict with Articles 10 and 23 of the Constitution.

who: People who owe overdue taxes or customs duties

raw.answer: A person had sued over the same dispute in both the administrative court and the civil courts, and each said it had no authority to hear it. The question was whether an administrative court precedent, which said state-run companies cannot be defendants in administrative lawsuits, violates the Constitution. The court held that it does not, because such disputes belong in civil court.
raw.held: A state-run enterprise set up as a company under the Company Act is a private-law entity, and a dispute with its staff over whether their contract has ended must go through civil litigation. The administrative court precedent is not unconstitutional, in substance meaning these cases are outside the administrative court's authority.

points.text: When someone's lawsuit is rejected by both administrative and civil courts for lack of jurisdiction, the court may accept the case and also resolve conflicting views connected to the precedent at issue.
A state-run enterprise set up as a company is a private legal entity with independent personhood, and it holds rights and duties in its own name.
Its relationship with its staff is a private-law contract, and dismissing someone is a private-law act of ending that contract, not an exercise of public power.

Even if the law requires government agencies to take part in decisions on hiring or review of staff, that is an internal supervisory relationship between the agency and the company and does not change the staff contract.
So a dispute over whether the contract has ended must go to civil court, not the administrative court.

The precedent's reasoning that only government agencies can be defendants conflicts with Interpretation No. 269 and is no longer applied. Its substance, that these cases are outside the administrative court's authority, does not limit civil remedies and so is not unconstitutional.

who: State-run companies set up under the Company Act
Staff assigned or appointed under Company Act Article 27 or other laws

raw.answer: The case asked whether a tax law and a Ministry of Finance letter were constitutional when they punished anyone who failed to properly attach a tax inspection or payment certificate as if they had evaded tax, even if no tax was actually evaded. The court found this went further than necessary and did not fit the constitution's protection of people's rights. It ordered that the provision and the letter no longer be applied.
raw.held: The part of the 1971 Commodity Tax Act that fined people two to ten times the evaded tax for not properly attaching required certificates, whether or not tax was evaded, and the Ministry of Finance's 1977 letter saying the same, must no longer be applied.

points.text: The rule was meant to prevent tax evasion and ensure taxes are properly collected.
Tax penalties come in two kinds: penalties for breaking a procedural duty (acting or failing to act) and penalties for actually evading tax.

Where no tax was evaded, punishing someone who only broke a duty to act or not act by using the evaded-tax formula goes beyond what is necessary, so it does not fit the constitution's protection of rights.
The Ministry of Finance letter, which said failure to attach the certificate is treated as tax evasion whether or not tax was evaded, rests on that same provision and also must not be applied.

who: People who failed to attach required tax certificates
Taxpayers fined as if they had evaded tax
Tax authorities that imposed these penalties

raw.answer: The case asked whether two government orders were unconstitutional for saying that only producing businesses, not other businesses, are exempt from income tax on the extra money (premium) raised when shares are issued above face value. The court decided the orders do not conflict with the constitutional principle that taxes must be based on law. It said the legislature may reasonably decide whether and how far such income is tax-exempt.
raw.held: The orders saying that non-producing businesses have no tax exemption on share-premium income do not conflict with the constitution's principle that taxation must rest on law (tax legality).

points.text: Under the income tax law, business income inside the country is taxed unless a law grants an exemption.
Share premium goes beyond the company's registered capital, is accumulated as a capital reserve, and can be used to issue new shares, so it counts as company income.
Because it is income, the legislature may reasonably decide whether it is exempt and how far the exemption extends.
The Statute for Encouragement of Investment, Article 25, exempts only producing businesses that set the premium aside as a reserve under company law.

The two orders say the company law gives no exemption for capital reserves and that exemption applies only where another law grants it; this matches the above, so it does not conflict with Article 19 of the Constitution.
A later statute widened the exemption beyond producing businesses to fit new economic conditions, which does not make the earlier legislative choice unconstitutional.

who: Companies issuing shares above face value

raw.answer: The case asked whether a Ministry of the Interior circular was unconstitutional. The circular set a time limit for landowners to ask the government to expropriate the leftover part of their land as well. The court decided the circular does not conflict with the Constitution.
raw.held: The circular says a request for joint expropriation of the remaining land should be made from the time of negotiation until one year after expropriation is completed, and late requests are not accepted. The court held this is necessary to carry out Article 217 of the Land Act and does not conflict with the Constitution.

points.text: Article 217 of the Land Act lets an owner request expropriation of a leftover part that is too small or oddly shaped to be used properly, but it sets no time limit for the request.
Article 219 of the Land Act lets the original owner take back the land at the original price if it is not used as planned, or not put to use within one year after expropriation is completed.
So an owner's request for joint expropriation cannot be without a time limit, and the limit cannot be longer than the one in Article 219.
Without a limit, the agency needing the land could not use it under the approved plan within the legal period, which would harm the public interest and delay settling people's rights.
The Ministry's circular carries out the intent of Article 219 and is necessary to carry out Article 217, so it does not conflict with the Constitution.

raw.answer: The case asked whether provinces and counties may draw up their own budgets for provincial police administration and county police guard work. The court said they may, for the work that is their own responsibility, and if money falls short they can ask for subsidies. Where the central government hands police matters to provinces and counties to carry out, the central government budgets for them and they need not budget again.
raw.held: Provinces and counties may set budgets under lawful procedure for the costs of provincial police administration and county police guard work. If funds are truly insufficient, they may request subsidies under the Police Act, with the central government subsidizing provinces (and directly governed cities) and provinces subsidizing counties (and cities).

points.text: The police system is handled by the central government, or handed to provinces and counties to carry out. For matters handed down, the central government may budget for them and provinces and counties need not budget again.
Carrying out provincial police administration and county police guard work falls within the powers of provinces and counties under the Constitution, so they may budget for the costs.
Some of this work must be uniform nationwide or touches central powers, so the Police Act says the central government plans the budget standards for local police bodies, and budgets must follow them.
If funds are truly insufficient, a subsidy may be requested: from the central government for provinces and directly governed cities, and from the province for counties and cities.
Local bodies may not change the purpose of a subsidy, but provincial, city and county councils may still lawfully oversee how it is used.

raw.answer: The case asked whether a provision of the Income Tax Act that fines withholding agents for breaking their duties is unconstitutional. The provision fines a private group or business NT$500 if it fails to file on time, or files inaccurately, the recipient information required by Article 89, paragraph 3. The court decided the fine does not conflict with the Constitution.
raw.held: The 1987 amended Article 111, paragraph 2 of the Income Tax Act imposes a NT$500 fine on a private group or business that fails to file on time, or files inaccurately, under Article 89, paragraph 3. The court held this is a sanction for breaching a legal duty to act, is necessary for the public interest, and does not conflict with the Constitution.

points.text: Under the Income Tax Act, a withholding agent must withhold tax when paying, pay it to the national treasury on time, and report to the tax authority with withholding certificates. If the payment is below the withholding threshold, the agent must still file the recipient's name and related details on time.
The fine applies to a private group or business that breaks the Article 89, paragraph 3 filing rule, and it is a sanction for failing to carry out a legal duty.

The withholding and filing duty is a legally imposed duty to act. It lets the state reliably obtain tax data, which is necessary for the public interest, so the fine does not conflict with the Constitution.

who: Private groups and businesses that pay income

raw.answer: The case asked whether, after the 1992 constitutional amendments, the Control Yuan (監察院) is still part of the country's parliament-equivalent and still has the sole power to investigate, and when the Legislative Yuan may demand documents. The court said the Control Yuan is no longer a central representative body, but its impeachment, censure and corrective powers and the investigation power that supports them still belong only to it. The Legislative Yuan may request reference materials and, when needed, original documents, but not in areas where state organs are constitutionally protected in exercising their powers independently.
raw.held: Earlier Interpretation No. 76 no longer applies to the Control Yuan, and its investigation power tied to impeachment, censure and correction stays exclusively with it. The Legislative Yuan may request materials and, by a plenary decision, original documents, which the requested body may refuse only on legal grounds or other proper reasons, and this is limited for independently exercised powers such as judicial opinions, exam grading, Control Yuan judgments and pending case files.

points.text: Interpretation No. 76 treated the bodies as a parliament-equivalent because their members were elected. After the amendment, Control Yuan members are nominated by the President and approved by the National Assembly, so it is no longer a central representative body and that ruling no longer applies to it.

The Constitution divides powers among five yuans, each a top state organ, so which body counts as a parliament is not tied to how powers are divided. The amendments did not change the five-yuan system or add to Legislative Yuan powers, so the Control Yuan's impeachment, censure, correction and related investigation powers remain exclusively its own.

Legislators can question officials and invite people to committees. If matters remain unclear, the Legislative Yuan may by decision request reference materials and, when needed, original documents, and the requested body may refuse only on legal grounds or other proper reasons.

State organs whose independent exercise of power is constitutionally protected, such as judges, examination officials and Control Yuan members, and prosecutors' investigation, which is closely tied to criminal trials, must be free of outside interference.

So judicial legal opinions, exam grading, Control Yuan decisions on impeachment or correction, and handling and files of cases not yet finally decided are limited from Control Yuan investigation, and for the same reason from Legislative Yuan document requests.

raw.answer: The case asked whether Taipei City's standards for compensating landowners for crops and trees on land that is expropriated violate the Constitution. The standards cap the number of flowers and trees per are of land that gets compensated. The court held that the cap is constitutional, but said authorities must still look carefully at individual cases where solid evidence shows the real, normal planting differs greatly from the standard.
raw.held: The Taipei rule limiting compensable flowers and trees per are, with no compensation for the excess, does not conflict with the Constitution. However, where firm evidence shows genuine, normal planting differs greatly from the standard, the authority must assess that case carefully using expertise and experience.

points.text: Under the land law article cited, compensation for improvements on expropriated land is estimated by the local land authority with other agencies, so it should reflect the actual specific condition of the improvements.

The land law lets authorities exclude from expropriation crops whose type or quantity clearly does not match normal planting, and some owners or users plant rashly or excessively once they know expropriation is coming, seeking unfair gain.
The Taipei City Government, acting within its authority as the responsible agency, set the standards to carry out that law.

Capping the number of flowers and trees and denying compensation for the excess is necessary to prevent such rush planting and to achieve fair compensation, so it does not conflict with the Constitution.

Because the cap reflects ordinary situations, in an individual case with firm evidence that real normal planting differs greatly from it, the authority must use its expertise to judge carefully whether there was rush or excessive planting.

who: Taipei City Government and land authorities

raw.answer: The case asked whether it is unconstitutional that the Urban Planning Act, as amended on 15 July 1988 (Article 50), sets no deadline for the government to acquire land reserved for public facilities. The court decided it is not unconstitutional, because it protects the integrity of the urban plan and serves the public interest. The court added that how to better protect landowners is a matter for the legislature.
raw.held: Article 50 of the Urban Planning Act, as amended on 15 July 1988, does not conflict with the Constitution in setting no acquisition deadline for reserved public facility land. How to revise the laws to balance landowners' interests is a legislative question.

points.text: Reserved public facility land is part of a whole urban plan, which is drawn up for expected development over 25 years, so the reserved land and the plan stand in a part-to-whole relationship.
Unless the plan is changed, a deadline cannot be set for one piece of reserved land, with the reservation deemed cancelled at expiry, without shaking the whole plan.

Changing an urban plan has its own procedures in the Act, which an advance acquisition deadline cannot replace; this differs from the Land Act rule on expired reserved expropriation, and the two are not special and general law.
So the rule protects the integrity of the plan, and carrying out the plan is necessary for the public interest, so it does not conflict with Articles 23 and 143 of the Constitution.
The plan must be reviewed at least every five years, and if reserved land is kept after review, the authority should acquire it promptly to avoid long reservation.

Without acquisition, owners cannot get payment or pursue other plans and use controls remain, so the land loses value and the burden grows over time; existing remedies do not compensate individual special sacrifice by length of reservation, so the legislature should consider revisions.

who: Owners of land reserved for public facilities
