raw.answer: The case asked whether a National Assembly extraordinary session that was not called for the purpose of amending the Constitution may amend it. The court decided it may not, because people should know in advance what an amendment aims at and have a chance to voice their views. It said its earlier Interpretation No. 29 must be supplemented accordingly.
raw.held: A National Assembly extraordinary session that was not convened for the purpose of amending the Constitution may not exercise the power to amend it, and Interpretation No. 29 is supplemented to that effect.

points.text: The Constitution is the nation's fundamental law, and amending it greatly affects constitutional order and public welfare, so citizens should know the purpose of an amendment beforehand and be able to express views.

Interpretation No. 29 dealt only with powers of the National Assembly at its regular sessions under Article 29; it did not mean an extraordinary session may use all powers regardless of why or how it was convened.
Advance knowledge also lets Assembly delegates gauge public opinion, so they can act in line with the public's reasonable expectations and trust.

Past practice, such as the Temporary Provisions and the Additional Articles, had the President convene extraordinary sessions specifically to discuss or make constitutional amendments, consistent with this principle.

Extraordinary sessions are convened under varying circumstances and procedures, unlike regular sessions, so a session called for another purpose may not bypass the constitutional limits on convening procedure to amend the Constitution.
Therefore sessions the President convenes under Additional Articles Article 11 paragraphs 1 and 2 and Article 15 may not amend the Constitution, and Interpretation No. 29 is supplemented.

raw.answer: The case asked whether Interior Ministry rules for issuing 'self-farming ability certificates' were unconstitutional because they judge who can farm land by where the person lives compared with where the land is. The court held that the location limits do not conflict with the Constitution. It added that the ministry should keep reviewing and revising the rules so farmers who can really farm the land are not harmed.
raw.held: The 1986 and 1990 versions of the Interior Ministry's rules, which limit the applicant's residence relative to the farmland acquired or taken back, do not conflict with the Constitution. The residence-based test for ability to farm should be reviewed and revised from time to time.

points.text: The Land Act and the Farmland Rent Reduction Act require that a buyer of private farmland, or a landlord taking back rented farmland, be able to farm it personally.
The Interior Ministry, within its authority, issued the certificate rules to carry out these laws, and revised them several times, including the location limits between residence and land.

The location limits (same or neighboring township, later same county or city or neighboring townships) rest on the then policy that farmland belongs to farmers who farm it, and take account of ordinary farming tools, so they do not conflict with the Constitution.
Because farming methods, transport and agricultural policy change, the residence or current-farmland test should be reviewed and revised so that farmers who can actually farm are not harmed.

who: Farmers able to farm in practice

raw.answer: The case asked whether an Interior Ministry directive was unconstitutional. The directive said a worker who retires, leaves the insurance and collects old-age benefits cannot also claim injury and illness benefits. The court found the directive consistent with the Constitution.
raw.held: The court held that the 1980 Interior Ministry directive is consistent with the intent of the ruling and does not conflict with the Constitution. A worker who has claimed old-age benefits should not also claim injury and illness benefits.

points.text: Injury and illness benefits are payments to help workers who cannot work because of injury or illness and so lose their usual pay.
Old-age benefits are payments to workers who retire and so no longer get wages. The ruling says this makes the two benefits the same in nature.
Because the two benefits are the same in nature, a worker who claims old-age benefits should not claim injury and illness benefits as well.

Article 20, paragraph 1 lets a worker keep claiming benefits for one year after insurance coverage stops. The ruling says retirement is not the only reason coverage can stop, so a retired worker who has already claimed old-age benefits is handled under the reasoning above.
The directive matches this reasoning, so it does not conflict with the Constitution.

who: Insured workers who retire and claim old-age benefits
Workers claiming injury or illness benefits after retiring

raw.answer: The case asked what counts as a "treaty" under the Constitution and which international agreements must be sent to the Legislative Yuan for review. The court said a treaty is a written international agreement with another country or international organization, whether called a treaty, convention or agreement, that directly concerns important national matters or people's rights and duties and has legal effect. It then set out which of these must go to the Legislative Yuan.
raw.held: Agreements called treaties or conventions, or agreements with a ratification clause, must be sent to the Legislative Yuan. Other written international agreements must also be sent, unless authorized by law, approved in advance by the Legislative Yuan, or their content matches existing domestic law.

points.text: The Constitution gives the President the power to conclude treaties, requires treaty proposals to go through the Executive Yuan meeting, and gives the Legislative Yuan the power to decide on treaty cases.
Treaties concluded under these rules rank the same as ordinary laws.

A treaty is a written international agreement, named a treaty or convention, or another name if its content directly concerns important national matters such as defense, foreign affairs, finance and the economy, or people's rights and duties, and has legal effect.

Agreements named treaty or convention, or with a ratification clause, must be sent to the Legislative Yuan; others must be too, unless authorized by law, approved beforehand, or matching domestic law.

Agreements not needing review, and other agreements outside treaty cases, are handled by the responsible agency through rule-making or ordinary administrative procedures, and the Foreign Ministry's handling rules must be revised accordingly.
Treaties involving a change of territory must also be decided by the National Assembly under Article 4, and agreements between Taiwan and mainland areas are outside this ruling.

who: Foreign Ministry and other responsible agencies
People whose rights and duties are affected by international agreements
